newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope will avoid politics in Poland, bishop says.
newsitem.headline: Pope will avoid politics in Poland, bishop says.

text.p: Pope John Paul ll will not comment on local politics during his coming visit to his native Poland but will speak out against abortion, a senior Polish bishop said on Wednesday.
"The Holy Father will not involve himself in our political debate," Tadeusz Pieronek, Secretary General of the Polish Roman Catholic episcopate, told an informal news conference.

The Pope's May 31 to June 10 trip will take place as campaigning heats up for parliamentary elections, due around September, which pit the Catholic, rightist Solidarity Election Action (AWS) against the secular-minded ruling ex-communists.

The campaign looks set to be fought partly around issues like abortion, which the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) has liberalised despite strong protests from the Church and the Pope himself.

Some analysts argue the Pope's visit will give heart and possibly votes to the AWS, which groups dozens of small rightist parties around the Solidarity union, which has said it will reverse the new more liberal abortion law if it wins power.
Pieronek said the Pope would not contribute to the divisions in Polish society but would raise ethical issues such as abortion, which the Church condemns.

"It is not the Pope's fault that in touching on such matters -- and I think he will refer to it -- he touches on politics. It is the fault of politicians who have politicised such ethical subjects," he said.
The Pope worked closely with Solidarity during the union's struggle leading to the 1989 fall of communism and has not hidden his continued sympathy for it.

Solidarity and other rightist parties have been agitating on the Church's behalf over issues including passage of a concordat treaty with the Vatican that has long been blocked by the leftist majority in parliament but seems near ratification.

Solidarity has called on Poles in a referendum on May 25, just before the Pope arrives, to reject a new draft constitution which has been agreed by major parliamentary parties but which the opposition grouping regards as too secular.
Leaders of the union, which has drafted an alternative constitution founded on Catholic values, had asked bishops to publicly pray for the government's draft to be defeated.
But the Church refused last week, saying God should not be asked to make political choices for people.

The Church hierarchy, which unsuccessfully opposed the election of ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski in 1995 presidential elections, now wants to preserve its authority to speak to all Poles rather than be linked with one faction.
This apolitical stance has caused disagreements within the Church and attacks on Pieronek by Catholic right-wingers.
